::: notes
The whole set of tools fits on one slide once you sort it by job rather than by brand family. First, something to analyse with – R, which is what we use, but Python and Julia are entirely reasonable choices for this work, and Stata and SPSS are still the default in a lot of departments. Second, somewhere to write it: Positron is what I will be driving on the shared screen, RStudio is the one that most of you will already know, VS Code does everything if you are willing to configure it, Jupyter is the notebook world. Third, publishing and sharing, which is the part that people skip. Quarto turns text and code into a document; git records every version with a date; GitHub hosts the repository so others can reach it; and OSF or Zenodo give the whole thing a permanent address with a DOI. Ringed in orange is what this course uses, and the rest is there so you know the alternatives.
:::

## Programming languages {#languages-what-you-are-actually-choosing .smaller .deepdive run="tools"}

::: {.toolgrid style="--cols: 4"}
<div class="tool ours"><img src="pics/tools/r.svg" alt="R"><span class="name">R</span><span class="what">Built by statisticians for data analysis. Hard to beat for models, tables and figures, thanks to its packages.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/python.png" alt="Python"><span class="name">Python</span><span class="what">A general language that also does data. Better for pipelines, scraping, text and machine learning.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/julia.png" alt="Julia"><span class="name">Julia</span><span class="what">Fast, young, small ecosystem. Worth it when your model takes hours.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/stata.svg" alt="Stata"><span class="name">Stata</span><span class="what">Excellent panel and survey estimators, superb docs, one syntax. Costs money and hides its source.</span></div>
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
You do not have to choose once and forever. Quarto runs R, Python and Julia chunks in the **same document**, and the course browser lab is R compiled to run inside a web page.
:::

::: notes
A slower look at the languages, because people agonise about this and mostly should not. R was built by statisticians for data analysis, and that is still where it wins, in models, tables and figures. Most of that comes from the package ecosystem: whatever obscure estimator your literature uses, someone has written the package. Python is a general-purpose language that also does data, so it is the better choice for pipelines, scraping, text and machine learning. Julia is fast and young with a small ecosystem, and earns its place when a model takes hours rather than seconds. Stata deserves respect – excellent panel and survey estimators, the best documentation in the business, one consistent syntax – and it costs money and hides its source. And none of this is a life choice, because Quarto will run R, Python and Julia chunks in the same document.
:::

## Editors and IDEs {#where-you-write-it .smaller .deepdive run="tools"}

::: {.toolgrid style="--cols: 5"}
<div class="tool ours"><img src="pics/tools/positron.png" alt="Positron"><span class="name">Positron</span><span class="what">The newer IDE from Posit. R and Python as equals, VS Code underneath.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/rstudio.svg" alt="RStudio"><span class="name">RStudio</span><span class="what">Still excellent, still supported. If it is what you know, use it.</span></div>

<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/jupyter.png" alt="Jupyter"><span class="name">Jupyter</span><span class="what">Notebook-first. Beware: cells can run out of order.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/neovim.png" alt="Neovim"><span class="name">Neovim</span><span class="what">For the keyboard-only. Steep to learn, and very fast once learned.</span></div>
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Of the choices in the toolchain, the editor matters least. It changes how *you* work and nothing about what a reader receives.

**A trap:** a notebook lets you run cells out of order, so it can show output that no clean run would produce. Restart and run everything before you believe it.
:::

::: {.src}
Positron and RStudio are both from Posit; both are free, and RStudio is open source.
:::

::: notes
The editor is the least consequential choice in the toolchain, so I will be quick. Positron is the newer environment from Posit, built on VS Code, treating R and Python as equals – it is what I will be driving on the shared screen. RStudio is still excellent and still supported, and if it is what you know, there is no reason to move. VS Code will do anything once you have configured it. Jupyter is notebook-first and Python-first. Neovim is for people who never want to touch a mouse. What matters is the trap in the second box, and it applies to every notebook-style tool including the interactive mode in Quarto: you can run cells out of order, which means the output on your screen may be output that no clean run would ever produce. Restart the session and run everything, top to bottom, before you believe a number.
:::

## Plain-text file formats {#plain-text-is-the-format-that-survives .smaller}

::: {.toolgrid style="--cols: 4"}
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/terminal.png" alt="R script"><span class="name">.R</span><span class="what">Code only, with prose in comments.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/markdown.png" alt="Markdown"><span class="name">.md</span><span class="what">Prose only. Headings, lists, links – no code.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/rmarkdown.png" alt="R Markdown"><span class="name">.Rmd</span><span class="what">Prose + R, rendered together. R only.</span></div>
<div class="tool ours"><img src="pics/tools/quarto.png" alt="Quarto"><span class="name">.qmd</span><span class="what">Prose + R, Python or Julia. The course format.</span></div>
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Every one of these is a **plain text file**. You can open it in anything, compare two versions of it line by line, email it, and read it in twenty years. A `.docx` with pasted output is not plain text, and nothing in it records which numbers came from which code.
:::

::: notes
Four file types, in increasing order of what they hold. A dot-R file is code with comments. A markdown file is prose with no code. An R Markdown file is prose and R together, rendered into one document. And a Quarto file is the same idea, except the code can be R or Python or Julia. What they have in common is that every one is a plain text file. You can open it in any editor, see exactly what changed between two versions, email it, and still read it in twenty years. Compare that with a Word document holding numbers you pasted in from somewhere. It looks the same on the page, but nothing in it records which number came from which line of code. That is how the old value of a number you have since recomputed can still be sitting in the paper.
:::

## What happens when you render {#how-a-document-becomes-a-document}

![](pics/tools/render-pipeline.png){fig-align="center" width="72%"}

::: {.small}
You write **one** source file. Rendering runs your code, inserts the results, and produces whatever output you asked for from that one source.
:::

::: notes
And this is what happens when you press render. You write one source file, with prose and code together. Knitr – or Jupyter, if you are working in Python – runs every chunk of code in a fresh session and replaces it with its actual output, giving a plain markdown file. Pandoc then turns that into whatever you asked for: a Word document for your co-author, a PDF for the journal, a web page for your project site, slides like these. So there is one place where a number is computed, and every output shows the same number, because they were all produced from the same source in the same run. When a reviewer asks you to drop three countries, you change one line and re-render, and the table, the figure and the sentence in the text all change together. That alone makes rendering worth learning, quite apart from anything to do with credibility.
:::

## The package layer {.smaller .deepdive run="tools"}

::: {.toolgrid style="--cols: 4"}
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/pkg-easystats.png" alt="easystats"><span class="name">easystats</span><span class="what">Data work with datawizard, and model output as tidy data: parameters, performance, effect sizes.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/pkg-tidyverse.png" alt="tidyverse"><span class="name">tidyverse</span><span class="what">Reading files, and the verbs that datawizard lacks. One grammar across all of it.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/pkg-modelsummary.png" alt="modelsummary"><span class="name">modelsummary</span><span class="what">Regression tables you can publish, from the fitted objects.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/pkg-marginaleffects.png" alt="marginaleffects"><span class="name">marginaleffects</span><span class="what">Predictions, contrasts and marginal effects from almost any model.</span></div>
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Your figures come from **`tinyplot`**, and the causal graphs from **`dagitty`**, which **`ggdag`** draws more neatly where it is installed. The setup page lists the full set, and the check script in your workspace reports anything that is missing.
:::

::: notes
A word about packages, because this is where the advantage of R actually lies. Easystats comes first in this course. Its datawizard package does the data work, filtering, selecting and summarising, and the rest of the family turns model output back into tidy data – coefficients, fit statistics, effect sizes – instead of the printed blob that summary gives you. The tidyverse reads the files and covers the few verbs that datawizard lacks. Modelsummary builds publication-ready regression tables straight from fitted model objects, so your table cannot disagree with your model. And marginaleffects computes predictions, contrasts and marginal effects from almost any model you can fit, which is how you get from a coefficient to a statement in the units that your reader thinks in. The figures that you draw come from tinyplot and the causal graphs from dagitty, and the check script in your workspace reports anything that is missing.
:::

## Version control {#version-control-in-one-slide .smaller .deepdive run="tools"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**Git** is a program on your machine. It records a **complete, dated snapshot** every time you say so, and it never forgets one.

**GitHub** is a website that hosts those snapshots so other people can reach them – and it is not the only one (GitLab, Codeberg, one hosted by your university).
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
What it gives you that a folder of `final_v3_REALLY_final.R` cannot:

- Every past state, recoverable exactly
- A written reason attached to each change
- A public, timestamped trail of when you knew what
- A way for two people to edit the same file without one overwriting the other
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
The tasks use **none of it**. There is a companion module on the site, and your workspace folder is the ideal thing to practise on.
:::

::: notes
Version control is the one tool that I have kept out of the tasks, so let me at least name it properly. Git is a program that runs on your machine: every time you tell it to, it records a complete dated snapshot of your project, and it never forgets one. GitHub is a website that hosts those snapshots so other people can reach them. It is not the only one: there is GitLab, there is Codeberg, and your university may run its own. What does that give you that a folder full of final-version-three-really-final does not? Every past state recoverable exactly, a written reason attached to every change, a public timestamped trail of when you knew what – which, notice, is a preregistration mechanism in itself – and a way for two people to work on one file without one silently overwriting the other. There is a companion module on the site.
:::

## Where data and code are archived {#where-data-and-code-go-to-live .smaller}

::: {.toolgrid style="--cols: 4"}
<div class="tool ours"><img src="pics/tools/osf.png" alt="OSF"><span class="name">OSF</span><span class="what">Projects, files, and registrations. Free, and it hosts the public records of SCORE and Multi100.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/zenodo.svg" alt="Zenodo"><span class="name">Zenodo</span><span class="what">CERN-run archive. Gives a DOI; takes a GitHub release directly.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/dataverse.svg" alt="Dataverse"><span class="name">Dataverse</span><span class="what">Institutional data archives with proper metadata and curation.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><span class="badge" style="--tint:#4a6741">XYZ</span><span class="name">Domain archives</span><span class="what">GESIS, UK Data Service, ICPSR – licensed access to survey microdata.</span></div>
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
**A repository is not an archive.** A GitHub repository can have its history rewritten, be renamed, or be deleted tomorrow. An archived deposit gets a **DOI**, a fixed version, and a commitment to keep serving it. Serious work usually needs both.
:::

::: notes
And the last group: where things go so they are still there in ten years. OSF is free, holds projects and files and registrations, and the public records of SCORE and Multi100 are kept there – you will read some of them later. Zenodo is run by CERN, gives you a DOI, and will take a GitHub release directly, which makes archiving a one-click habit. Dataverse is the institutional data-archive world with proper metadata and curation. And then the domain archives – GESIS, the UK Data Service, ICPSR – which is where licensed survey microdata is held. A repository is not an archive, although people often treat it as one. A GitHub repository can have its history rewritten, be renamed or be deleted tomorrow, and the link in your paper dies. An archived deposit has a DOI, a fixed version and an institution committed to serving it. Serious work usually needs both.
:::

## Licences, briefly {.smaller .deepdive run="tools"}

::: {.small}
| What | Common choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Code** | MIT · GPL | MIT: use it however you like. GPL: and share your changes back |
| **Data** | CC0 · CC BY | CC0 puts it in the public domain; CC BY asks for attribution |
| **Text, figures, slides** | CC BY · CC BY-NC | Attribution, optionally no commercial reuse |
| **Someone else's data** | *their* terms | Licensed survey microdata usually may not be passed on, by me or by you |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Publishing with no licence is not a neutral default. It means **all rights reserved** – legally, nobody may reuse the work at all.
:::

::: notes
Licensing gets skipped and then bites. Four rows. For code, MIT says use it however you like, GPL says use it and share your changes back. For data, CC-zero puts it in the public domain and CC-BY asks for attribution. For text and figures and slides, CC-BY or CC-BY with a non-commercial clause. And the fourth row is the one that most often constrains a reanalysis: when the data are not yours, their terms govern. Much survey microdata is held under a licence that lets you analyse it and forbids you to pass it on, so a replication package can carry the code and point to the archive, but not the file itself. A dataset released under CC-zero, by contrast, can travel with the code, and anyone can rerun the analysis without asking anyone. And the line at the bottom: leaving a repository without a licence does not make it free to use. Legally it means all rights reserved, so nobody may reuse it at all.
:::
